article.title: Brazilian Communist Parties React to Lula’s Electoral Victory and Bolsonaro’s Flight to the US
article.author: MLToday
article.content: By Nikos Mottas October 30, 2026 In Defense of Communism EDITOR’S NOTE: Brazil has three Communist Parties. The PCdoB is part of the Lula governing coalition. The PCB and PCBR are not. Brazil’s communist parties have responded to the re-election of social-democrat Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the subsequent flight of defeated far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro to the United States, warning that the electoral defeat of Bolsonarism does not eliminate the threat of reactionary forces, coup attempts and imperialist interference.In separate statements, the Brazilian Communist Party (PCB) and the Brazilian Revolutionary Communist Party (PCBR) stressed the necessity of mass mobilization and independent working-class struggle, while offering distinct assessments of the post-election political situation. Lula’s victory in the October 25 presidential runoff followed an intense electoral confrontation with Bolsonaro, who had finished ahead in the first round. The outcome was followed by Bolsonaro’s departure for the United States, despite a Brazilian Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports amid an ongoing investigation. In a statement issued on October 29, the PCB described Lula’s victory as a significant blow to the Brazilian far right and to the ambitions of US imperialism in Latin America. However, it warned that the conservative composition of Congress and the continuing influence of reactionary political forces meant that the struggle was far from over. The party expressed particular concern over Bolsonaro’s flight to the United States and his subsequent claims to be Brazil’s legitimately elected president. According to the PCB, the protection afforded to the defeated candidate by Donald Trump’s administration could become an instrument of political pressure against Brazil. Washington, it warned, might exploit allegations of political persecution to challenge the legitimacy of the election results, attack Brazilian institutions and encourage new destabilization campaigns. The PCB also raised concerns about the possible role of Argentine President Javier Milei’s government in facilitating Bolsonaro’s departure, pointing to the broader cooperation between Latin American far-right forces and US imperialism. Calling for the defense of the electoral result and national sovereignty, the party emphasized that resistance to neofascism must also confront neoliberalism, capitalist exploitation and the policies of class collaboration. A day earlier, on October 28, the Central Committee of the PCBR had issued its own assessment, placing particular emphasis on the decisive role of popular mobilization in Bolsonaro’s electoral defeat. According to the PCBR, the political turnaround between the two rounds was driven largely by spontaneous demonstrations involving workers, students and young people. These mobilizations, it argued, represented a rejection of Bolsonarism rather than an endorsement of Lula’s political programme. The revolutionary communists warned that the far right retained substantial political strength, including in Congress and state governments, and accused reactionary forces of attempting to obstruct voting and subsequently discredit the election results. The PCBR cautioned that these maneuvers could create conditions for another coup attempt and potentially provide a pretext for US intervention. At the same time, the party rejected any suggestion that Lula’s victory should lead workers to abandon their political independence. It characterized the Lula–Alckmin administration as a government of class collaboration, criticizing its fiscal austerity policies, concessions to capital and commitment to maintaining the existing bourgeois political order. Both parties had supported a vote for Lula against Bolsonaro in the second round, without abandoning their criticism of the social-democratic government or endorsing its political programme.
